description:
As Al Jazeera English marks its 20th anniversary, correspondent Tony Cheng reflects on two decades of reporting across Asia, from covering China's changing society in Beijing at the channel's launch in 2006 to reporting from Tibet, Xinjiang and Sichuan. He recalls witnessing the growing assertiveness of Chinese communities, including villagers protesting against officials after the 2008 Sichuan earthquake, while documenting the continued grip of the authorities. Cheng also looks back at the 2009 Red Shirt protests in Bangkok, when the Thai army fired live rounds at demonstrators, and more recent coverage of Myanmar's civil war, which has taken a devastating toll on civilians. From political upheaval and conflict to the unexpected impact of flooding in Bangkok, Cheng reflects on the unpredictability of reporting across the region and the experiences that have shaped his 20 years with Al Jazeera English.

description:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is delivering its judgment in a landmark genocide case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar over the military crackdown on the Rohingya in 2017.

The court has examined evidence of mass killings, forced displacement, sexual violence and other abuses against the Rohingya, with hundreds of thousands fleeing to Bangladesh. The central legal question is whether Myanmar's military acted with the specific intent to destroy the Rohingya, in whole or in part.

The ruling is being closely watched by Rohingya refugees seeking justice and by international legal experts, particularly because of its potential implications for other genocide cases before the court, including South Africa's case against Israel.

Al Jazeera's Steph Vassen reports from The Hague, while Tanvir Chowdhury speaks to Rohingya activists in Bangladesh.

author: Al Jazeera English
description: Al Jazeera correspondent Haru Mutasa reflects on two decades of reporting across Africa, from her first live broadcast in Darfur, Sudan, on the day Al Jazeera English launched in 2006, to covering conflict, political upheaval and the birth of South Sudan. She recalls reporting on protests, post-election violence, arrests and economic turmoil in Zimbabwe, as well as witnessing South Sudan’s independence in 2011. Mutasa says seeing events unfold on the ground has brought both professional challenges and deeply human experiences, particularly when reporting from conflict zones. One encounter in South Sudan stands out: a woman who had been sheltering at home during fighting gave her a bracelet to thank Al Jazeera for keeping her informed. The experience reinforced the importance of being present, reporting from local communities and giving people a voice.
